text:
Throughout this module, you've been looking more and more closely at
what an agent does while completing a task.

You started with individual actions, then looked at the sequence of
actions in a trajectory, and finally,

at requirements that can stretch across several
turns of a conversation.

But even if all of that looks right, there's still one question left:
Did the agent actually do what it said it would?

In the dog shelter case, suppose a volunteer asks,
"Can you book me with Pepper for Saturday at 2 PM?"

The agent checks the volunteer's eligibility,
confirms that Pepper is available, and then responds, "Great,
you're booked with Pepper for Saturday at 2 PM."

So far, everything looks good, but if you really want to know
whether the task succeeded,
the agent's message isn't the final source of truth.

You need to check the booking system. Is there actually a booking for
this volunteer and Pepper on Saturday at 2:00?

If the row exists with the right volunteer, dog, date, and time,
then the outcome matches what the agent claimed.

But imagine the agent gives exactly the same confirmation,
and you check the booking system and there's nothing there.

Now you have a different kind of failure. The response says the
booking succeeded, but the state of the system says it didn't.

That's why, for tasks that are supposed to change something outside
the conversation, you often need to evaluate the outcome directly.

Northwind gives you a similar example.
Suppose a customer asks for a refund on order 4521.

The agent verifies the customer, looks up the order,
determines that the refund is allowed, calls the refund tool,
and then tells the customer, "Your refund has been processed."

Again, that sounds like success, but instead of trusting the message,
check the refunds table in the system of record.

Is there now a refund for order 4521?
Does it belong to the right customer? Is the amount correct?

If the customer was supposed to receive $49.99, you can compare
that expected amount with the value that was actually written.

That gives you evidence about the final state of the task, rather than
evidence about what the agent intended to do or what it said happened.

And because that state is structured, a very simple deterministic
evaluator is usually enough.

You don't need an LLM to read the conversation and guess whether the
refund probably happened when you can ask the database directly.

For example, if the expected outcome is a $49.99
refund for order 4521,

your evaluator can look for a refund row with that
order ID and amount.

If it finds a row, the outcome passes. If the agent says the refund
was processed, but no matching row exists, it fails.

And sometimes the outcome you want is that nothing changes. Suppose
the customer asks for a refund on an order that isn't eligible.
In that case, you don't want to find a new refund row at all.

So after the interaction, you can check the same system and confirm
that no refund was created.
That makes outcome evaluation useful in both directions.

You can verify that an expected change happened, and you can verify
that an action that should have been blocked never changed the system.
Now, here's where this gets especially useful.

An outcome evaluator and a trajectory evaluator can look at the exact
same run and reach different conclusions.

Take the Northwind refund case. The customer asks for a
refund on order 4521.

The agent processes a $49.99 refund, and when you check the refunds
table, the row is there.
Right order, right amount, so the outcome evaluator passes.
From the point of view of the final state, the task succeeded,

but then you inspect the trajectory and it turns out the agent looked
up the order and called process_refund
before it verified the customer.

only after the refund had already been issued did it retrieve
the customer record.
So now you have two pieces of evidence that tell you different things.

The outcome check says yes, the refund exists
and the amount is correct.

The identity before refund check says no, the agent didn't follow the
required policy before issuing it. Both results are useful.

The outcome tells you that the agent produced the intended state,
and the trajectory tells you that it took the wrong path to get there.

And that distinction matters because a successful outcome doesn't
automatically mean the run was acceptable.

Let's imagine an equivalent example for the shelter. A booking exists
for Pepper at the right time, so the outcome looks correct.

But if the agent skipped the eligibility check before creating it,
the shelter may still consider the booking invalid.
The final state is there, but the process wasn't executed as required.

This is why it's useful to keep the outcome and process
evaluations separate.

If you collapse them into one overall "did the task succeed" result,
you lose information about what actually happened.

A run where the agent followed every required step but failed to
create the final booking is different from a run where the booking
exists but the agent violated policy along the way.

Those failures may eventually need very different fixes. And there's
another advantage to checking the system of record directly.
Remember the general rule we've been using throughout this module:

match the evaluator to the evidence that can actually
answer the question.

If you want to know whether the agent chose order_lookup,
inspect the tool call.

If you want to know whether customer verification happened
before the refund, inspect the trajectory.

If you want to know whether a standing instruction from three turns
ago was respected, inspect the session.

And if you want to know whether the refund really exists,
inspect the refunds table.

Giving an evaluator more conversation text won't make it better at
answering a question the database can answer directly.

So at this point, you have several different views of the same agent
task. You can look at the response the user sees.

You can inspect the individual actions the agent chose. You can
reconstruct the trajectory and see how those actions fit together.

You can look across a session when earlier turns
still matter, and now,

you can even check the external state to see what the
task actually changed.
None of those views replaces the others.

Each of them answers a different question, and that means they can
disagree in ways that are actually very informative.

In the final video of this module, you'll bring those evaluation
layers together around complete Northwind runs.

You'll see how a response can pass while a tool call fails,
how the outcome can be correct while the process violates policy,

and how those different results help you locate where a
complex task broke down.

That will give you the full evaluation picture you'll carry into the
improvement stage in module 5.
